    MULTIDIMENSIONAL NMR · STUDENT EXPERIMENTS

    3D NMR laboratory

    Explore HN/N/C backbone correlations or HN/N/Hx proton correlations in TOCSY-HSQC and NOESY-HSQC. The synthetic AGSLVA peptide is uniformly ¹³C/¹⁵N labelled; the proton experiments require ¹⁵N editing.

    ILLUSTRATIVE DATA

    Switch on the console, choose an experiment, then prepare the labelled peptide.

    Procedure & interpretation

    1. Switch on the console and select a triple-resonance experiment.
    2. Prepare the uniformly ¹³C/¹⁵N-labelled peptide model: Ala–Gly–Ser–Leu–Val–Ala (AGSLVA), in a conceptual 90% H₂O / 10% D₂O sample.
    3. Acquire: the teaching sequence loads the tube, locks the instrument, samples two indirect dimensions, and processes the three-dimensional dataset.
    4. Rotate the peak view and choose a ¹⁵N slice. Click a cross-peak or peak-list row to identify the participating atoms.
    5. Compare HNCA with HN(CO)CA to distinguish Cα(i) from Cα(i−1). Use HNCO to connect the amide to the preceding carbonyl.
    6. For HNCACB, compare Cα and Cβ signals of opposite sign. Glycine has no Cβ.
    7. In TOCSY-HSQC, identify Hα, Hβ and side-chain H within one spin system. Compare mixing times and reacquire.
    8. In NOESY-HSQC, distinguish self, intra-residue, sequential and hypothetical long-range contacts. Do not interpret scalar TOCSY cross-peaks as distances.

    Sample times and intensities are compressed for teaching. Coordinates are illustrative shifts; this exercise does not simulate a complete pulse sequence or real instrument sensitivity.

    Worked sequential assignment

    For Ser3 (HN = 8.15 ppm, N = 116.2 ppm), HNCA gives Cα = 58.5 ppm (Ser3) and 45.0 ppm (Gly2). HN(CO)CA retains only Gly2 at 45.0 ppm. HNCO links Ser3 to Gly2 carbonyl at 173.5 ppm. Thus the predecessor is Gly2. Ser Cβ at 63.0 ppm is downfield of its Cα; chemical-shift order alone does not identify Cα versus Cβ.

    Worked proton-correlation example

    Ser3 at HN 8.15 / N 116.2 ppm gives TOCSY correlations to Hα 4.45 and Hβ 3.85 / 3.95 ppm. NOESY additionally includes a sequential Gly2 Hα contact at 3.92 ppm and an assumed long-range Ala6 HN contact at 8.25 ppm. The latter is a hypothetical proximity example; no folded conformation was derived.

    University of Pittsburgh: triple-resonance pathways · Example of protein backbone assignment · Northwestern: 3D NOESY-HSQC acquisition · Muhandiram & Kay: heteronuclear-edited NOESY

    Applications of NMR 06

    Explore how NMR supports research, industry, medicine and forensic science. These are real-world applications; the teaching model demonstrates basic NMR concepts rather than the specialist experiments described here.

    1. Drug discovery2. Pharmaceutical industry3. Food chemistry4. Medical applications5. Controlled drugs analysis

    1. Drug Discovery

    NMR is an established method in early-stage drug discovery. It can detect weak interactions, including binding with millimolar dissociation constants under suitable experimental conditions, without requiring prior knowledge of a protein’s biological function. [1]

    • Fragment-Based Drug Discovery (FBDD): Screens libraries of small molecular fragments for binding to a disease-related target. Binding fragments provide starting points for compounds with improved affinity and selectivity. [2]
    • Target- vs. Ligand-Observed Screening: Ligand-observed methods such as STD (Saturation Transfer Difference) and WaterLOGSY detect changes in ligand signals associated with binding. Target-observed experiments follow changes in the protein’s signals. SAR-by-NMR uses chemical-shift perturbations and structural information to guide fragment optimization; shifts indicate affected environments, not necessarily direct contacts. [1] [2]
    • Evaluating Physico-Chemical Properties: Appropriate NMR experiments can measure solubility, pKa, and partitioning expressed as log P or log D7.4. These measurements support drug development, but generally require distinct experimental conditions rather than one universal simultaneous measurement. [3]

    2. Pharmaceutical Industry

    NMR supports quality control, manufacturing, formulation and characterization of active pharmaceutical ingredients (APIs). [1] [4]

    • Structural Elucidation: COSY reveals through-bond proton correlations, HSQC links protons to directly bonded heteronuclei (commonly carbon), and HMBC reveals longer-range correlations. Together, these establish molecular connectivity. Spatial information and 3D structure assessment typically also require experiments such as NOESY or ROESY and additional constraints. [1]
    • Polymorph and Solid-State Analysis: Solid-state NMR distinguishes local environments in crystalline polymorphs and amorphous forms. Combined with complementary methods, it helps assess formulation stability and forms that influence dissolution and bioavailability. [1]
    • Impurity Profiling: NMR detects and characterizes impurities or residual solvents when their signals are resolved and sufficiently intense. Quantitative NMR (qNMR) can determine amounts using a suitable calibrated reference without a separate authentic standard for every analyte. It complements liquid chromatography, although very low-level impurities can fall below NMR’s sensitivity. [4]

    3. Food Chemistry

    NMR provides reproducible chemical profiles for food quality assessment, supply-chain verification and food-fraud investigation. [5] [6]

    • Food Authentication and Origin Mapping: Chemical fingerprints, interpreted using validated reference databases and statistical models, can help distinguish geographic origin, plant variety or harvest year in products such as extra virgin olive oil, honey, wine and coffee. Classification reliability depends on representative reference samples. [5] [6]
    • Adulteration Detection: Profiles can reveal added sugar syrups in honey, cheaper seed oils blended into olive oil, or changes consistent with milk dilution. Detection depends on the adulterant, concentration, sample preparation and validated method; it is not automatically instantaneous or conclusive for every sample. [5] [6] [7]
    • Shelf-Life and Oxidation Tracking: Repeated measurements monitor changes in edible fats, oxidation products and nutritional components during storage or transit, supporting assessment of rancidity and product stability. [5]

    4. Medical Applications

    NMR spectroscopy investigates biological samples, while magnetic resonance imaging applies related nuclear-spin physics to the living body.

    • Magnetic Resonance Imaging (MRI): Magnetic fields, radiofrequency pulses and spatial gradients generate non-invasive, detailed images of soft tissues, organs and tumors without ionizing radiation. MRI uses the same underlying nuclear magnetic resonance principles with specialized imaging hardware and protocols. [8]
    • Metabolomics & Biomarker Discovery: Spectral profiles of blood plasma, urine or cerebrospinal fluid identify and quantify many metabolites, depending on concentration and signal overlap. Comparing profiles helps investigate metabolic pathways and candidate biomarkers for cancer, metabolic disease and organ dysfunction. Proposed diagnostic markers require independent clinical validation. [1]
    • In-Cell NMR: Specialized experiments observe molecules within living cells, including human cells, to investigate target engagement, structural changes and, where feasible, binding kinetics. Applicability depends on signal sensitivity, cellular conditions and often labeling or controlled target expression. [9] [10]

    5. Controlled Drugs Analysis

    Forensic laboratories use NMR and qNMR to identify substances, determine purity and investigate chemical similarities between seized samples. [11]

    • Identification of Novel Psychoactive Substances (NPS): 1D and 2D NMR help elucidate structures of unfamiliar synthetic cannabinoids, cathinones and other designer drugs. This is particularly valuable when reference spectra are unavailable. Mass spectrometry can also provide evidence for unknown compounds; combining methods strengthens identification. [11]
    • Purity Testing and Batch Profiling: qNMR can determine the purity of seized substances such as cocaine, heroin and MDMA using validated acquisition and calibration. Comparing cutting agents and impurities can support links between seizures, alongside other forensic evidence; similar profiles alone do not prove a shared manufacturing source. [4] [11]
    • Isotopic Fingerprinting: Specialized isotope-ratio NMR, including site-specific natural isotopic fractionation by 2H NMR (SNIF-NMR), can provide evidence about origin or production history. Geographic attribution requires suitable reference data and validated models. Routine 13C or 2H spectra do not by themselves establish plant versus laboratory origin or a precise geographic source. [12]
